paras: The lynching of Jack Harris was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Clarendon, Arkansas, shortly after midnight on June 25, 1903. Harris, accused of assaulting his white landlord John Coburn, was taken from a guard with whom the sheriff had hidden him in a barn. Arkansas papers described the sheriff's failed ruse in detail, and a week later Black tenants near Coburn's farm received anonymous letters telling them to leave.

According to the reports, Harris assaulted Coburn, a white planter living eight miles east of Clarendon, on the Sunday night before the lynching, breaking one of his arms. A Brinkley dispatch to the New York Sun said Coburn had rebuked Harris for using a mule all day without permission, and that Harris fled when Coburn's wife came with a gun. Harris was captured the next day and jailed at Clarendon.

The Newport Daily Independent linked the lynching to an earlier case in the same neighborhood, where a Black man named Riley Park had killed a white man named Fowler and a mob had failed to lynch him. The paper suggested Harris would not have met "such severe measures" otherwise, and added that local Black residents were "said to have grown very insolent" since then.

Shortly after midnight, a mob of about fifty men called at the home of Deputy Sheriff John Black and demanded the jail keys. The men were "supposed to have been the friends and neighbors" of Coburn. Expecting trouble, Sheriff Milwee had already moved Harris to a barn under one guard, named by the Newport paper as William Swift and called a deputy elsewhere, and he let the mob search the empty jail. Meanwhile another party found Harris and his guard in the barn and took the prisoner.

Swift, whom the mob held until the hanging was over, said the crowd was orderly and sober, and that Harris was allowed to pray until he grew too loud. The first attempt to hang him failed when the rope gave way as a buggy was driven from under him; he was then drawn up by hand and died of strangulation.

The Newport paper said the lynching was deplored by many citizens, and no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage. On July 1 a Clarendon dispatch reported that Black residents of the "Fowler-Coburn neighborhood" had received anonymous letters saying that "the quickest way out of the country was the best." Landlords persuaded the tenants to stay on promises of protection, and the paper attributed the letters to white renters hoping a labor shortage would cheapen rents.

Arkansas papers carried the fullest accounts, led by the Newport Daily Independent's "Negro Lynched by Clarendon Mob," which relied on the guard's picture of an orderly crowd. The same account of the hanging ran as "Lynching at Clarendon" in the Monticellonian, the Forrest City Times and the Van Buren Press, while the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic gave it one sentence.

Outside the state, the St. Louis Republic headed its special "Jack Harris Hanged for Assaulting White Man," and the New York Sun's "Lynched for Breaking an Arm" called it "a lynching bee." A short wire item reached papers from Kansas to Washington and Louisiana, and every white account treated the assault on Coburn as fact without giving Harris's side.

In the Black press the lynching appears only as a line in the Indianapolis Freeman's list of June lynchings, which placed it at Brinkley. The Freeman introduced the list by noting that June "has been considered the month of fatalities, deaths, destructions."

The Sun's Brinkley dispatch put the lynching at about 7 a.m. and the mob at about fifteen masked men, while the Clarendon reports gave 1 a.m. or just after midnight and about fifty men. The Sun placed the hanging at the porch of the American Cotton Company's office, the wire item at a porch in the suburbs, and the Monticellonian at a wagon-yard shed.

bases: A mob of about fifty (fifteen in one report) took Jack Harris from a guard to whom the sheriff had entrusted him and hanged him (A2, A4, A7, A13).

Harris was taken from a sheriff's guard by a mob of fifteen to fifty men and hanged without any legal process (A2, A4, A7); the mob acted as friends of the white man he was accused of assaulting (A2, A13).

A Clarendon special to the St. Louis Republic, a Brinkley dispatch to the New York Sun and the Newport Daily Independent's Clarendon report independently agree that Harris was taken from a guard and hanged by a mob (A2, A4, A7).

accounts.gist: Swift said the mob was orderly and sober, let Harris pray, and hanged him on a second attempt after the rope gave way.

accounts.gist: Fifty masked men took Harris from a deputy in a barn at 1 a.m. while part of the mob searched the jail; a member had spied on the sheriff.

accounts.label: Brinkley dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: About fifteen masked men hanged Harris at about 7 a.m. to the porch rafters of the American Cotton Company's office; the assault followed a dispute over a mule.

accounts.label: Arkansas weekly account
accounts.gist: About fifty friends of Coburn hanged Harris to a rafter in a wagon-yard shed after locating him and the deputy in the barn.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: A mob of fifty hanged Harris to the porch of a building in the suburbs; he had seriously injured Coburn.

accounts.label: Black press list
accounts.gist: The Freeman's list of June lynchings records Jack Harris at Brinkley, Ark., June 25.

framing.detail: Newport's 'NEGRO LYNCHED BY CLARENDON MOB' narrated the sheriff being outwitted, relayed the guard's view of an orderly crowd, said Black residents had grown 'very insolent', and noted the affair was deplored by many citizens.
The Sun's 'LYNCHED FOR BREAKING AN ARM' called it 'a lynching bee' and gave the mule dispute as cause.
St. Louis Republic ('Jack Harris Hanged for Assaulting White Man'), the wire brief and digests stated the assault as fact without comment.
The Freeman recorded Harris only as a line in its June lynching list, introduced as 'the month of fatalities, deaths, destructions'.

conflicts.note: Three reports, two datelined Clarendon, agree on after midnight; the Sun's Brinkley dispatch stands alone.
The fifty figure may count the whole mob at the jail; the Sun may count the party at the hanging. Not resolved in the coverage.

quotes: The men are supposed to have been the friends and neighbors of John Coburn, the white man who sustained serious injuries at the hands of a negro named Jack Harris.
Mr. Swift, whom the mob kept with them till after the job was finished, says that the crowd was orderly, there being no one under the influence of drink.
Since then the negroes are said to have grown very insolent in the Coburn neighborhood. The affair is deplored by many citizens here.
